proofs.proof_tex:
Put \(\overline f_{mathrm{pre}}=n^{-1}\sum_{t=1}^n f_t\) and \(\overline f_{\mathrm{post}}=m^{-1}\sum_{t=n+1}^{n+m}f_t\).  We first record a consequence of \(\texttt{ass:geometric-beta-mixing}\) and \(\texttt{ass:moment-bound}\) that will be used repeatedly.  If two scalar functions of the primitive process, separated by \(j\) periods, have uniformly bounded \((2+\epsilon)\)-moments, truncating both functions at level \(\beta_n(j)^{-1/(2+\epsilon)}\), applying the total-variation definition of absolute regularity to the bounded parts, and applying H\"older's inequality to the tails gives
\[
 \left|\operatorname{Cov}_{P_n}(G_t,H_{t-j})\right|
 \leq C\beta_n(j)^{\epsilon/(2+\epsilon)}
 \leq C\exp(-c j).
\]
Here and below \(C,c\in(0,\infty)\) depend only on the fixed moment and mixing bounds.  All coordinates and products used below have such moments because \(u_{s,t}\), \(\psi_{s,t}\), and the entries of \(Z_{s,t}W_{D_s,t}^{\prime}\) are polynomials of degree at most two in \(X_t\), while \(\texttt{ass:moment-bound}\) supplies a uniform \((8+\delta_0)\)-moment.  Summing the preceding covariance bound therefore gives, for every centered such process \(G_t\),
\[
 \operatorname{Var}_{P_n}\!\left(N^{-1}\sum_{t=1}^N G_t\right)
 \leq \frac{1}{N}\sum_{j\in\mathbb Z}
       \left|\operatorname{Cov}_{P_n}(G_0,G_j)\right|
 \leq \frac{C}{N}.
\]
Consequently all empirical first and second moments used below differ from their expectations by \(O_{P_n}(N^{-1/2})\).  Strict stationarity in \(\texttt{ass:stationarity}\) makes the expectations independent of the location of the block.

Fix \(s\in\mathcal S\).  By the definition of \(\alpha_s\),
\[
 \mathbb E_n u_{s,t}
 =\mathbb E_n[Z_{s,t}Y_t(0)]-M_s\alpha_s=0.
\]
On the event that \(\widehat M_s\) is invertible, the empirical bridge equation gives the exact identity
\[
 \widehat M_s(\widehat\alpha_s-\alpha_s)
 =\overline u_{s,\mathrm{pre}},
 \qquad
 \widehat\alpha_s-\alpha_s
 =\widehat M_s^{-1}\overline u_{s,\mathrm{pre}}.
\]
The preceding moment bound gives
\[
 \widehat M_s-M_s=O_{P_n}(n^{-1/2}),
 \qquad
 \overline u_{s,\mathrm{pre}}=O_{P_n}(n^{-1/2}).
\]
By \(\texttt{ass:bridge-rank}\), \(\lVert M_s^{-1}\rVert_{\mathrm{op}}\leq\kappa^{-1}\).  Hence
\[
 \Pr_{P_n}\!\left\{\lVert\widehat M_s-M_s\rVert_{\mathrm{op}}<\kappa/2\right\}\longrightarrow1,
\]
and on this event \(\lVert\widehat M_s^{-1}\rVert_{\mathrm{op}}\leq2/\kappa\).  The resolvent identity then yields
\[
 \widehat M_s^{-1}-M_s^{-1}
 =-M_s^{-1}(\widehat M_s-M_s)\widehat M_s^{-1}
 =O_{P_n}(n^{-1/2}).
\]
It follows that the fixed measurable fallback is used with probability tending to zero and
\[
 \widehat\alpha_s-\alpha_s
 =M_s^{-1}\overline u_{s,\mathrm{pre}}+O_{P_n}(n^{-1})
 =M_s^{-1}n^{-1}\sum_{t=1}^n u_{s,t}+o_{P_n}(n^{-1/2}).
\]

Before treatment \(Y_t=Y_t(0)\), and after treatment \(Y_t=Y_t(0)+\Delta_t\).  Thus the definition of \(\widehat\tau_s\) gives the exact decomposition
\[
 \widehat\tau_s-\tau
 =\overline v_{s,\mathrm{post}}
  -(\overline W_{D_s,\mathrm{post}})^{\prime}
       (\widehat\alpha_s-\alpha_s).
\]
The process \(v_{s,t}\) is centered: by \(\texttt{ass:bridge-centering}\) and the definition \(\tau=\mathbb E_n\Delta_t\),
\[
 \mathbb E_n v_{s,t}
 =\mathbb E_n[Y_t(0)-W_{D_s,t}^{\prime}\alpha_s]
  +\mathbb E_n\Delta_t-\tau=0.
\]
Moreover, \(\overline W_{D_s,\mathrm{post}}-\mu_s=O_{P_n}(m^{-1/2})\).  Since \(n/m\to r\in(0,\infty)\) by \(\texttt{ass:sample-ratio}\), multiplication of the two root-sample-size errors gives
\[
 (\overline W_{D_s,\mathrm{post}}-\mu_s)^{\prime}
       (\widehat\alpha_s-\alpha_s)=O_{P_n}(n^{-1})=o_{P_n}(n^{-1/2}).
\]
Using \(H_s=-\mu_s^{\prime}M_s^{-1}\) and \(\psi_{s,t}=H_su_{s,t}\), we therefore obtain
\[
 \sqrt n(\widehat\tau_s-\tau)
 =n^{-1/2}\sum_{t=1}^n\psi_{s,t}
  +\sqrt{\frac nm}\,m^{-1/2}\sum_{t=n+1}^{n+m}v_{s,t}
  +o_{P_n}(1).
\]
Because \(\mathcal S=\{1,2\}\) is finite, taking the maximum of the two remainders proves both expansions uniformly over \(s\in\mathcal S\).  The covariance-limit assumption ensures that every variance named in these expansions has the finite limit used in the statement.

Fix \(s\in\mathcal S\), and first consider either true centered scalar score \(w_t=\psi_{s,t}\) on a block of length \(N=n\), or \(w_t=v_{s,t}\) on a block of length \(N=m\).  The centering of \(\psi_{s,t}\) follows from \(\mathbb E_nu_{s,t}=0\), and that of \(v_{s,t}\) was proved in \(\texttt{lem:fixed-role-linearization}\).  The primitive \((8+\delta_0)\)-moment bound gives a uniform \((4+\epsilon)\)-moment for \(w_t\), for some \(\epsilon>0\).  The truncation argument in that lemma therefore gives
\[
 |\gamma_{w,n}(j)|
 :=|\operatorname{Cov}_{P_n}(w_t,w_{t-j})|
 \leq C e^{-cj},
 \qquad j\geq0.
\]

Let \(\widetilde\gamma_N(j)=N^{-1}\sum_{t=j+1}^Nw_tw_{t-j}\).  If two summands in this average overlap, their covariance is bounded by a constant; there are at most \(C N(j+1)\) ordered overlapping pairs.  Otherwise the two pairs of observations are separated by a distance \(h\geq1\), and the same truncation argument, now applied to the two products, bounds their covariance by \(Ce^{-ch}\).  Summation over all ordered pairs gives
\[
 \operatorname{Var}_{P_n}\{\widetilde\gamma_N(j)\}
 \leq C\frac{j+1}{N}.
\]
For a Bartlett cutoff \(q\), the triangle and Cauchy--Schwarz inequalities imply
\[
 \mathbb E_n\left|
   \sum_{|j|\leq q}\left(1-\frac{|j|}{q+1}\right)
   \{\widetilde\gamma_N(j)-\mathbb E_n\widetilde\gamma_N(j)\}
 \right|
 \leq C\sum_{j=0}^q\sqrt{\frac{j+1}{N}}
 \leq C\frac{q^{3/2}}{\sqrt N}.
\]
The deterministic truncation, Bartlett-weight, and finite-block biases obey
\[
 \sum_{|j|>q}|\gamma_{w,n}(j)|
 +\frac{1}{q+1}\sum_{|j|\leq q}|j|\,|\gamma_{w,n}(j)|
 +\frac{1}{N}\sum_{|j|\leq q}|j|\,|\gamma_{w,n}(j)|
 \leq C\{e^{-cq}+q^{-1}+N^{-1}\}.
\]
Replacing the true zero mean by the sample mean changes the Bartlett quadratic form by \(O_{P_n}(qN^{-1/2})\); this follows by expanding every centered product, using \(\overline w=O_{P_n}(N^{-1/2})\), and applying Cauchy--Schwarz to the at most \(2q+1\) diagonals.  Thus the oracle centered Bartlett estimator satisfies
\[
 \widehat\Omega^{\mathrm{or}}_{w}
 -\sum_{j\in\mathbb Z}\gamma_{w,n}(j)
 =O_{P_n}\!\left(
      \frac{q^{3/2}}{\sqrt N}+\frac q{\sqrt N}
      +\frac1q+e^{-cq}
   \right).
\]
For \(q=q_n=\lfloor\min(n,m)^{1/5}\rfloor\), \(\texttt{ass:sample-ratio}\) implies that every term on the right tends to zero for both \(N=n\) and \(N=m\).  By \(\texttt{ass:covariance-limit}\), the two infinite covariance sums converge to \(\Omega_{\psi,s}\) and \(\Omega_{v,s}\), respectively.  Hence the oracle Bartlett estimates converge in probability to those limits.

It remains to justify the fitted scores in \(\texttt{def:conventional-selected-att}\).  The proof of \(\texttt{lem:fixed-role-linearization}\) gives \(\widehat\alpha_s-\alpha_s=O_{P_n}(n^{-1/2})\) and \(\widehat M_s-M_s=O_{P_n}(n^{-1/2})\).  In addition,
\[
 \widehat\mu_s^{\mathrm{post}}-\mu_s=O_{P_n}(m^{-1/2}),
 \qquad
 \widehat H_s-H_s=O_{P_n}(n^{-1/2}),
\]
where the second assertion follows from the resolvent identity, the bridge-rank margin, and \(n/m\to r\).  On the event where the empirical inverse exists,
\[
 \widehat u_{s,t}-u_{s,t}
 =-Z_{s,t}W_{D_s,t}^{\prime}(\widehat\alpha_s-\alpha_s),
\]
and hence, using the tight empirical second moments supplied by \(\texttt{ass:moment-bound}\),
\[
 \left\{n^{-1}\sum_{t=1}^n
   (\widehat\psi_{s,t}-\psi_{s,t})^2\right\}^{1/2}
 =O_{P_n}(n^{-1/2}).
\]
Similarly, on the post block,
\[
 \widehat v_{s,t}-v_{s,t}
 =-W_{D_s,t}^{\prime}(\widehat\alpha_s-\alpha_s)
  -(\widehat\tau_s-\tau),
\]
and the fixed-role expansion gives
\[
 \left\{m^{-1}\sum_{t=n+1}^{n+m}
   (\widehat v_{s,t}-v_{s,t})^2\right\}^{1/2}
 =O_{P_n}(n^{-1/2}).
\]
The normalized Bartlett quadratic-form matrix has operator norm at most \(2q_n+1\).  Therefore, if \(\widehat w=w+e\),
\[
 |\widehat\Omega_{\widehat w}-\widehat\Omega_w|
 \leq (2q_n+1)
 \left[2\left\{N^{-1}\sum_tw_t^2\right\}^{1/2}
          \left\{N^{-1}\sum_te_t^2\right\}^{1/2}
       +N^{-1}\sum_te_t^2\right]
 =O_{P_n}(q_n n^{-1/2})=o_{P_n}(1).
\]
The same estimate covers empirical centering.  The fallback events have probability tending to zero by the bridge-rank argument.  We have proved
\[
 \widehat\Omega_{\psi,s}\to_{P_n}\Omega_{\psi,s},
 \qquad
 \widehat\Omega_{v,s}\to_{P_n}\Omega_{v,s}.
\]
Finally, \(n/m\to r\) gives
\[
 \widehat V_s^{\mathrm{conv}}
 =\widehat\Omega_{\psi,s}+\frac nm\widehat\Omega_{v,s}
 \to_{P_n}\Omega_{\psi,s}+r\Omega_{v,s}=V_s.
\]
There are only two roles, and \(V_s\geq\nu\) by \(\texttt{ass:att-variance-margin}\).  Thus
\[
 \Pr_{P_n}\!\left\{\min_{s\in\mathcal S}
       \widehat V_s^{\mathrm{conv}}\geq\nu/2\right\}
 \geq
 1-\sum_{s=1}^2
 \Pr_{P_n}\{|\widehat V_s^{\mathrm{conv}}-V_s|>\nu/2\}
 \longrightarrow1,
\]
which also proves asymptotic positivity.

For role \(s\), write the empirical ridge criterion as
\[
 \widehat Q_s(a)
 =\overline{Y(0)^2}_{\mathrm{pre}}-2a^{\prime}\widehat b_s
   +a^{\prime}\widehat K_sa,
 \quad
 \widehat b_s=\overline{W_{D_s}Y(0)}_{\mathrm{pre}},
 \quad
 \widehat K_s=I_{d_s}+\overline{W_{D_s}W_{D_s}^{\prime}}_{\mathrm{pre}}.
\]
Because \(\widehat K_s\succeq I_{d_s}\), its minimizer is unique and equals \(\widehat a_s=\widehat K_s^{-1}\widehat b_s\).  The moment and mixing assumptions give \(\widehat a_s-a_s=O_{P_n}(n^{-1/2})\).  Completing the square around the empirical minimizer yields the exact identity
\[
 \widehat L_s
 =\widehat Q_s(a_s)
  -(\widehat a_s-a_s)^{\prime}\widehat K_s(\widehat a_s-a_s).
\]
Since \(\lVert\widehat K_s\rVert_{\mathrm{op}}=O_{P_n}(1)\), the last term is \(O_{P_n}(n^{-1})\).  By the definition of \(\ell_{s,t}\),
\[
 \sqrt n(\widehat L_s-L_s)
 =n^{-1/2}\sum_{t=1}^n(\ell_{s,t}-L_s)+o_{P_n}(1).
\]
Consequently \(\texttt{ass:local-loss-gap}\) and the stipulated joint Gaussian limit imply
\[
 \sqrt n(\widehat L_1-\widehat L_2)
 \Rightarrow d+Q_1-Q_2=d+D.
\]
By \(\texttt{ass:selector-variance-margin}\), \(D\) is a normal variable with variance at least \(\nu\), so \(\Pr(d+D=0)=0\), even if the full joint Gaussian covariance matrix is singular.  More explicitly, for every \(\varepsilon>0\), the normal density bound gives
\[
 \Pr\{|d+D|\leq\varepsilon\}
 \leq \frac{2\varepsilon}{\sqrt{2\pi\nu}}.
\]
Approximate the indicator of \(( -\infty,0]\) from above and below by continuous functions that differ only on \([-\varepsilon,\varepsilon]\).  Joint convergence of the loss coordinate makes the corresponding expectations converge, while the preceding boundary-strip bound vanishes as \(\varepsilon\downarrow0\).  The tie-breaking rule in \(\texttt{def:ridge-selector}\) consequently gives
\[
 \widehat J\Rightarrow J(d),
 \qquad J(d)=\mathbf 1\{d+D\leq0\}+2\mathbf 1\{d+D>0\}.
\]

Simultaneously, \(\texttt{lem:fixed-role-linearization}\), the assumed joint pre-period Gaussian limit, the assumed independent post-period Gaussian limit, and \(n/m\to r\) give
\[
 \left(\sqrt n(\widehat\tau_1-\tau),
       \sqrt n(\widehat\tau_2-\tau),
       \sqrt n(\widehat L_1-\widehat L_2)\right)
 \Rightarrow
 \left(A_1+\sqrt rR_1,A_2+\sqrt rR_2,d+D\right).
\]
The switching map is discontinuous only when its last coordinate is zero.  On the complement of the preceding \(\varepsilon\)-strip it is continuous; within the strip, tightness of the two ATT coordinates first restricts them to a compact set with arbitrarily high probability.  Continuous upper and lower interpolations on that compact set, followed by \(\varepsilon\downarrow0\), therefore transfer the joint convergence through the switch.  Since
\[
 \sqrt n(\widehat\tau_{\mathrm{sel}}-\tau)
 =\sum_{s=1}^2 \mathbf 1\{\widehat J=s\}
   \sqrt n(\widehat\tau_s-\tau),
\]
this boundary-strip argument proves
\[
 \sqrt n(\widehat\tau_{\mathrm{sel}}-\tau)
 \Rightarrow A_{J(d)}+\sqrt rR_{J(d)}.
\]

By \(\texttt{lem:conventional-hac-consistency}\),
\[
 \max_{s\in\mathcal S}|\widehat V_s^{\mathrm{conv}}-V_s|
 \to_{P_n}0,
 \qquad
 \Pr_{P_n}\{\min_s\widehat V_s^{\mathrm{conv}}>0\}\to1.
\]
Thus selection cannot amplify the variance-estimation error, because
\[
 |\widehat V_{\widehat J}^{\mathrm{conv}}-V_{\widehat J}|
 \leq\max_s|\widehat V_s^{\mathrm{conv}}-V_s|=o_{P_n}(1).
\]
On the event \(\min_s\widehat V_s^{\mathrm{conv}}\geq\nu/2\), the inverse-square-root map is Lipschitz with a constant depending only on \(\nu\).  The selected numerator is \(O_{P_n}(1)\), and therefore replacing \(\sqrt{V_{\widehat J}}\) by \(\sqrt{\widehat V_{\widehat J}^{\mathrm{conv}}}\) changes the studentized statistic by \(o_{P_n}(1)\).  Using \(\widehat{\operatorname{se}}_s^{\mathrm{conv}}=\sqrt{\widehat V_s^{\mathrm{conv}}/n}\) and the same boundary-strip argument now gives
\[
 \frac{\widehat\tau_{\mathrm{sel}}-\tau}
      {\widehat{\operatorname{se}}_{\widehat J}^{\mathrm{conv}}}
 \Rightarrow
 \frac{A_1+\sqrt rR_1}{\sqrt{V_1}}\mathbf 1\{X\leq k\}
 +\frac{A_2+\sqrt rR_2}{\sqrt{V_2}}\mathbf 1\{X>k\}
 =T_1\mathbf 1\{X\leq k\}+T_2\mathbf 1\{X>k\},
\]
because \(d+D\leq0\) is equivalent to \(X\leq-d/\sigma_D=k\).  If a role is fixed, the same display contains only its single centered standard-normal coordinate.  If the standardized population gap diverges to either sign, tightness of the loss fluctuation makes one selection probability tend to one, giving the same fixed-role limit.  Finite \(d\), in contrast, leaves both role probabilities strictly between zero and one; this is precisely the additional local selection regime covered by the theorem.

Each \(T_s=(A_s+\sqrt rR_s)/\sqrt{V_s}\) is marginally standard normal.  The independent centered Gaussian post coordinate is included in this covariance statement, and \(\rho_s=\operatorname{Corr}(T_s,X)\).  In particular, \(\Pr(T_s=\pm z)=0\).  The boundary of the selected event \(\{|T_{J(d)}|\leq z\}\) is contained in \(\{T_1=\pm z\}\cup\{T_2=\pm z\}\cup\{X=k\}\), which has probability zero by the marginal variance assumptions.  Continuous upper and lower approximations to its indicator therefore show from \(\texttt{thm:selected-gaussian-limit}\) that the finite-sample Wald coverage converges to the probability calculated below.  For \(|\rho_s|<1\), completing the square in the joint Gaussian density gives
\[
 T_s\mid X=x\sim N(\rho_sx,1-\rho_s^2),
\]
so
\[
 \Pr\{|T_s|\leq z\mid X=x\}
 =\Phi\!\left(\frac{z-\rho_sx}{\sqrt{1-\rho_s^2}}\right)
  -\Phi\!\left(\frac{-z-\rho_sx}{\sqrt{1-\rho_s^2}}\right)
 =g_{\rho_s}(x;z).
\]
The selected limit in \(\texttt{thm:selected-gaussian-limit}\) chooses role one on \(\{X\leq k\}\) and role two on its complement.  Conditioning on \(X\), whose density is \(\phi\), therefore proves
\[
 \Pr\{|T_1|\leq z,X\leq k\}
 +\Pr\{|T_2|\leq z,X>k\}
 =\int_{-\infty}^{k}\phi(x)g_{\rho_1}(x;z)\,dx
  +\int_k^{\infty}\phi(x)g_{\rho_2}(x;z)\,dx
 =C_z(k).
\]
The formulas for \(|\rho_s|=1\) follow by weak convergence as \(|\rho_s|\uparrow1\), equivalently by using the degenerate conditional law \(T_s=\rho_sX\).

For every \(\rho\in[-1,1]\), symmetry of the interval gives
\[
 g_\rho(-x;z)=g_\rho(x;z),
 \qquad
 \int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\phi(x)g_\rho(x;z)\,dx
 =\Pr\{|T|\leq z\}=2\Phi(z)-1.
\]
Thus each half-line through zero contains one half of the unselected symmetric coverage, and
\[
 C_z(0)=\frac12\{2\Phi(z)-1\}
       +\frac12\{2\Phi(z)-1\}=2\Phi(z)-1.
\]

It remains to prove both necessity and the strict sign.  For \(a>0\) and \(q\in[0,1]\), let
\[
 R_z(a,q)=\Pr_q\{|X|\leq a,\ |T|\leq z\},
\]
where \((X,T)\) is bivariate standard normal with nonnegative correlation \(q\).  Because symmetric rectangles are unchanged by replacing \(T\) with \(-T\), \(R_z(a,q)\) depends on a correlation only through its absolute value.  For \(0<q<1\), let \(f_q\) denote the bivariate standard-normal density.  Direct differentiation of its displayed exponential formula gives
\[
 \frac{\partial f_q(x,t)}{\partial q}
 =\frac{\partial^2f_q(x,t)}{\partial x\,\partial t}.
\]
Integrating this identity over \([-a,a]\times[-z,z]\) and evaluating the four corners yields
\[
 \frac{\partial R_z(a,q)}{\partial q}
 =2\{f_q(a,z)-f_q(a,-z)\}.
\]
Moreover,
\[
 \frac{f_q(a,z)}{f_q(a,-z)}
 =\exp\!\left(\frac{2qaz}{1-q^2}\right)>1
 \qquad(a,z,q>0).
\]
Hence \(R_z(a,q)\) is strictly increasing in \(q\) on \([0,1]\), with strictness at zero and continuity at one obtained by integrating the positive derivative over every nonempty subinterval and then taking limits.

Using the evenness already proved, for every \(k\ne0\),
\[
 C_z(k)-\{2\Phi(z)-1\}
 =\frac{\operatorname{sign}(k)}{2}
 \left[R_z(|k|,|\rho_1|)-R_z(|k|,|\rho_2|)\right].
\]
Strict monotonicity gives
\[
 \operatorname{sign}\!\left(C_z(k)-[2\Phi(z)-1]\right)
 =\operatorname{sign}\!\left(k(\rho_1^2-\rho_2^2)\right).
\]
If \(\rho_1^2=\rho_2^2\), then \(g_{\rho_1}=g_{\rho_2}\) because conditional symmetric coverage depends only on the absolute correlation, and consequently \(C_z(k)=2\Phi(z)-1\) for every \(k\).  Conversely, if coverage is nominal for every \(k\), the strict sign formula rules out unequal squared correlations.  This proves the asserted if-and-only-if frontier and all endpoint cases.

We first derive, rather than assume, the properties of the construction in \(\texttt{def:primitive-gaussian-family}\).  Give role one donor \(W_{1t}=c_1(F_t+e_{1t})\) and proxy \(W_{2t}=c_{2,n}(F_t+e_{2t})\), and exchange these assignments for role two.  At the tied limit, write \(c_j=t_j^{-1/2}\).  Independence and \(B=\mathbb E_nF_t^2=\mu^2+f\) give, for both roles,
\[
 M_s=c_1c_2B,
 \qquad
 \alpha_1=\frac{c_2B}{c_1c_2B}=\frac1{c_1},
 \qquad
 \alpha_2=\frac{c_1B}{c_1c_2B}=\frac1{c_2}.
\]
Therefore
\[
 Y_t(0)-W_{1t}\alpha_1=e_{0t}-e_{1t},
 \qquad
 Y_t(0)-W_{2t}\alpha_2=e_{0t}-e_{2t},
\]
and both residuals have mean zero.  This proves both bridge equations and \(\texttt{ass:bridge-centering}\).  Moreover, \(\Delta_t=\tau+\xi_t\) implies \(\mathbb E_n\Delta_t=\tau\), so for either role
\[
 \mathbb E_n\{Y_t(0)+\Delta_t-W_{jt}\alpha_j\}=\tau.
\]
Thus the observed residual mean identifies the causal target in this family; the equality is a consequence of the bridge calculation, not a definition of \(\tau\).  Since the bridge matrix is scalar, its singular value is
\[
 |M_s|=c_1c_2B=\frac{B}{\sqrt{t_1t_2}},
\]
which is strictly larger than \(\kappa\) on \(\Theta_{\mathcal G}^{\mathrm{leg}}\).

For a donor \(W_j=c_j(F+e_j)\), its population ridge coefficient satisfies
\[
 a_j=\frac{c_jB}{1+c_j^2(B+\operatorname{Var}(e_j))},
 \qquad
 W_j a_j
 =\frac{B}{t_j+B+\operatorname{Var}(e_j)}(F+e_j).
\]
The equality \(t_2=t_1+x-y\) makes both denominators equal to
\(R=t_1+B+x=t_2+B+y\), so both prediction loadings equal \(\eta=B/R\).  Completing the population ridge square gives
\[
 L_j=\mathbb E_nY_t(0)^2
 -\frac{B^2}{t_j+B+\operatorname{Var}(e_j)},
\]
and hence \(L_1=L_2\) at the tied limit.  Along the stated local calibration, put
\[
 \delta_n=\frac{R^2}{B^2}\frac d{\sqrt n},
 \qquad t_{2,n}=t_2-\delta_n.
\]
Then \(t_{2,n}>0\) eventually and
\[
 L_1-L_2
 =\frac{B^2}{R-\delta_n}-\frac{B^2}{R}
 =\frac d{\sqrt n}\frac{R}{R-\delta_n}
 =\frac d{\sqrt n}+O(n^{-1}).
\]
Thus \(\sqrt n(L_1-L_2)=d+O(n^{-1/2})\), proving the local-gap premise without changing either bridge identity.

At the tied limit set \(U=(1-\eta)F+e_0\).  Centering the difference of the two ridge losses gives
\[
 D=-2\eta U(e_1-e_2)
   +\eta^2(e_1^2-e_2^2+y-x).
\]
The donor means are \(c_j\mu\), so the bridge sensitivities and pre-ATT scores reduce to
\[
 \psi_1=-K(F+e_2)(e_0-e_1),
 \qquad
 \psi_2=-K(F+e_1)(e_0-e_2),
 \qquad K=\frac\mu B.
\]
The post residuals are
\[
 v_1=e_0-e_1+\xi,
 \qquad v_2=e_0-e_2+\xi.
\]
All displayed processes are independent over time, so their long-run covariances equal their one-period covariances and the pre and post Gaussian limits are independent.

We now calculate the five quantities used by \(\Gamma\).  The two terms in \(D\) are uncorrelated by the vanishing odd moments of centered Gaussian variables.  Since
\[
 \mathbb E U^2=(1-\eta)^2B+b,
 \quad
 \mathbb E(e_1-e_2)^2=x+y,
 \quad
 \operatorname{Var}(e_1^2-e_2^2)=2(x^2+y^2),
\]
we get
\[
 \sigma_D^2
 =4\eta^2\{(1-\eta)^2B+b\}(x+y)
  +2\eta^4(x^2+y^2).
\]
For the first covariance, conditioning first on \((F,e_0)\) gives
\[
 \mathbb E\!\left[(e_1-e_2)(F+e_2)(e_0-e_1)\mid F,e_0\right]
 =-xF-ye_0.
\]
The quadratic part of \(D\) has zero covariance with \(\psi_1\), again by odd Gaussian moments.  Therefore
\[
 c_{D1}=\operatorname{Cov}(D,A_1)
 =-2\eta K\{(1-\eta)Bx+by\}.
\]
The analogous conditional calculation for role two yields
\[
 c_{D2}=\operatorname{Cov}(D,A_2)
 =2\eta K\{(1-\eta)By+bx\}.
\]
Finally, independence of the factors in each product gives
\[
 \operatorname{Var}(A_1)=K^2(B+y)(b+x),
 \quad
 \operatorname{Var}(A_2)=K^2(B+x)(b+y),
\]
and
\[
 \operatorname{Var}(R_1)=b+x+\zeta,
 \qquad
 \operatorname{Var}(R_2)=b+y+\zeta.
\]
Thus
\[
 V_1=K^2(B+y)(b+x)+r(b+x+\zeta),
 \qquad
 V_2=K^2(B+x)(b+y)+r(b+y+\zeta),
\]
and \(\rho_s=c_{Ds}/\sqrt{\sigma_D^2V_s}\), exactly as asserted by \(\Gamma\).

At the symmetric point \((\mu,f,b,x,y,\zeta,t_1,t_2)=(1,1,1,1,1,1,1,1)\),
\[
 B=2,\quad R=4,\quad\eta=K=\frac12,\quad
 \sigma_D^2=\frac{13}{4},\quad c_{D1}=-1,\quad c_{D2}=1,
 \quad V_1=V_2=\frac32+3r.
\]
Hence \(\rho_1=-\rho_2\).  For every finite local gap, Gaussian regression on \(D=\sigma_DX\) gives
\[
 \mathbb E\{A_{J(d)}+\sqrt rR_{J(d)}\}
 =\frac{c_{D2}-c_{D1}}{\sigma_D}\phi(k)
 =\frac{2}{\sigma_D}\phi(k)>0,
\]
while \(\texttt{thm:wald-symmetry-frontier}\) gives exact symmetric coverage for every \(k\).  Moreover \(B/\sqrt{t_1t_2}=2>\kappa\), \(\sigma_D^2=13/4>\nu\), and \(V_s>3/2>\nu\).  The stipulated bound on \(C_{\mathrm{mom}}\) gives the strict Gaussian moment inequality, so this point is legal for every \(r>0\).

At the asymmetric point in the statement,
\[
 B=2,\quad R=4,\quad\eta=K=\frac12,
 \quad \frac{B}{\sqrt{t_1t_2}}=\frac{10}{3},
\]
and substitution into the formulas just proved gives
\[
 \sigma_D^2=\frac{161}{100},\qquad
 c_{D1}=-\frac{19}{100},\qquad
 c_{D2}=\frac{91}{100},
\]
\[
 V_1=\frac14\frac{19}{5}\frac3{10}
      +\frac1{10}\frac4{10}=\frac{13}{40},
 \qquad
 V_2=\frac14\frac{11}{5}\frac{19}{10}
      +\frac1{10}(2)=\frac{249}{200}.
\]
Thus
\[
 \rho_1=-0.2626630497187030329\ldots,
 \qquad
 \rho_2=0.6427525060282437885\ldots,
 \qquad \rho_1^2<\rho_2^2.
\]
The inequalities \(10/3>\kappa\), \(161/100>\nu\), \(13/40>\nu\), and \(249/200>\nu\), together with the stated strict Gaussian moment bound, prove legality.  For \(d/\sigma_D=-1\), one has \(k=1\).  With \(z=\Phi^{-1}(0.95)\), direct substitution into the already proved one-dimensional integral gives
\[
 C_z(1)=0.8858209104904335667026974385\ldots.
\]
For completeness, this decimal is obtained without simulation by substituting the exact rational covariances above into the two error-function integrals, truncating at \(|x|=12\), whose omitted probability is at most \(2\Phi(-12)<4\times10^{-33}\), and evaluating the compact integrals at sixty-decimal working precision.  Repeating the calculation after subdividing each compact interval gives the displayed digits.  Independently of numerical quadrature, \(k>0\) and \(\rho_1^2-\rho_2^2<0\), so the strict sign theorem proves strict undercoverage analytically.

At this point \(R^2/B^2=4\), hence \(t_{2,n}=1/5-4d/\sqrt n\), as claimed.  Every bridge, variance, moment, and positivity expression above is continuous in \((\theta,d)\) wherever \(t_{2,n}>0\).  All legality inequalities at the asymmetric point are strict, and so are \(k>0\) and \(\rho_1^2<\rho_2^2\).  They therefore persist on a relatively open neighborhood of \((\theta,d)\) in the tied manifold crossed with the local-drift line, and they persist eventually along every corresponding local array.  The sign theorem gives strict undercoverage throughout that neighborhood.  Exchanging labels exchanges the squared-correlation ordering.  Keeping the roles fixed and reversing the sign of \(d\) changes the sign of \(k\), so the same sign theorem gives strict overcoverage.

If role \(s\) is fixed before observing the panel, \(\texttt{lem:fixed-role-linearization}\) and the Gaussian-limit premise used by \(\texttt{thm:selected-gaussian-limit}\) give
\[
 \sqrt n(\widehat\tau_s-\tau)\Rightarrow A_s+\sqrt rR_s,
 \qquad
 \frac{\widehat\tau_s-\tau}
      {\widehat{\operatorname{se}}_s^{\mathrm{conv}}}
 \Rightarrow T_s\sim N(0,1).
\]
Consequently its symmetric Wald coverage converges to \(2\Phi(z)-1\).  The same reduction occurs under diverging loss separation.  Indeed, the ridge expansion in \(\texttt{thm:selected-gaussian-limit}\) shows that
\[
 \sqrt n(\widehat L_1-\widehat L_2)
 =\sqrt n(L_1-L_2)+D_n+o_{P_n}(1),
 \qquad D_n=O_{P_n}(1).
\]
If \(\sqrt n(L_1-L_2)\to+\infty\), then \(\Pr(\widehat J=2)\to1\); if it tends to \(-\infty\), then \(\Pr(\widehat J=1)\to1\).  Substitution into the selected expansion therefore gives the corresponding fixed-role normal and nominal-coverage limit.

For the separated construction, fixing the role, or having the early selector choose it with probability tending to one, removes only the random label from \(\texttt{def:gap-split-estimator}\).  The remaining operations are exactly: estimate that role's bridge on \(\mathcal B_n\), average its residual on \(\mathcal C_n\), and estimate the two long-run variances on those same blocks.  Since
\[
 |\mathcal B_n|
 =n-\lfloor\varrho n\rfloor-\lceil(\log n)^2\rceil
 =(1-\varrho)n+o(n),
\]
the fixed-role linearization on these retained blocks has, under \(\sqrt n\)-normalization, variance
\[
 V_s^{\mathrm{gap}}
 =\frac{\Omega_{\psi,s}}{1-\varrho}+r\Omega_{v,s},
\]
rather than the full-pre-period variance \(V_s=\Omega_{\psi,s}+r\Omega_{v,s}\).  In fact,
\[
 V_s^{\mathrm{gap}}-V_s
 =\frac{\varrho}{1-\varrho}\Omega_{\psi,s}\geq0,
\]
with equality only when the pre-bridge influence has zero long-run variance.  Thus the construction reduces to ordinary fixed-role late-block proximal inference with its declared split-sample variance; it does not assert recovery of the full-pre-period efficiency bound.

By the definition of \(V_s^{\mathrm{gap}}\) and the definition of \(V_s\),
\[
\begin{aligned}
V_s^{\mathrm{gap}}-V_s
&=\left\{(1-\varrho)^{-1}-1\right\}\operatorname{Var}(A_s)
  +r\operatorname{Var}(R_s)-r\operatorname{Var}(R_s)\\
&=\frac{\varrho}{1-\varrho}\operatorname{Var}(A_s).
\end{aligned}
\]
The declared restriction \(0<\varrho<1\) makes \(\varrho/(1-\varrho)>0\), and every variance is nonnegative.  Consequently
\[
V_s^{\mathrm{gap}}=V_s+\frac{\varrho}{1-\varrho}\operatorname{Var}(A_s)\geq V_s.
\]
Assumption \(\mathrm{ass{:}att\mbox{-}variance\mbox{-}margin}\) states, separately for each \(s\in\mathcal S\), that \(V_s\geq\nu\).  Combining the last two displays proves the claim for both roles.  No rank or joint-covariance inversion is used.

theorem.statement:
The asserted whole-array uniform selector-conditional convergence is false under \(\mathcal M(D_{\mathrm{gap}})\) as defined.  More precisely, for admissible fixed positive margins there is, for every sufficiently large integer \(q\), a whole triangular array \((P_j^{(q)})_{j\geq1}\in\mathcal M(0)\) such that \(\operatorname{Var}(D)=39/625\), \(V_s^{\mathrm{gap}}=V_s=1\) for every \(s\in\mathcal S\), and the stacked limiting covariance is singular, but, with
\[
T_q=\frac{\widehat\tau_{\mathrm{gap}}-\tau}{\widehat{\operatorname{se}}_{\widehat J_A}},
\]
one has
\[
\liminf_{q\to\infty}
\mathbb E_{P_q^{(q)}}\!\left[
 \sup_{x\in\mathbb R}
 \left|\Pr_{P_q^{(q)}}\{T_q\leq x\mid\mathcal F_A\}-\Phi(x)\right|
\right]\geq\frac12.
\]
Thus positive limiting marginal variances and coordinatewise studentization do not compensate for the absence of a uniform finite-row variance and distributional-stabilization condition.
theorem.proof_tex:
We construct an explicit diagonal witness.  Set the post-period length in row \(j\) equal to \(m_j=j\), so the sample-ratio assumption holds with \(r=1\).  Fix \(\kappa=1/4\), \(\nu=1/100\), arbitrary positive geometric-mixing constants, and a moment envelope larger than the finite primitive moment calculated below.  Since the construction is independent over time, its absolute-regularity coefficients are zero and hence satisfy the declared geometric beta-mixing assumption for those constants.

For each sufficiently large integer \(q\), define a whole array \((P_j^{(q)})_{j\geq1}\).  In every row let the observations be independent and identically distributed over \(t\).  Let \((U_t,E_t,F_t)\) be centered Gaussian with
\[
\operatorname{Var}(U_t)=\operatorname{Var}(E_t)=\operatorname{Var}(F_t)=1,
\qquad
\operatorname{Cov}(E_t,F_t)=\frac12,
\]
and let \(U_t\) be independent of \((E_t,F_t)\).  Put
\[
Y_t(0)=U_t,qquad
A_t=(U_t+E_t,E_t)^{\prime},qquad
B_t=(U_t+F_t,F_t)^{\prime}.
\]
The controls comprise the four coordinates in \((A_t^{\prime},B_t^{\prime})^{\prime}\).  Role \(1\) uses donor vector \(A_t\) and proxy vector \(B_t\), whereas role \(2\) uses donor vector \(B_t\) and proxy vector \(A_t\).  These are two predeclared, disjoint, square donor/proxy assignments.

Let \(I_t\) be Bernoulli with success probability \(p_q=q^{-2}\), let \(\xi_t\sim N(0,1)\), and make \((I_t,\xi_t)\) independent of all controls.  The treatment-effect coordinate in row \(j\) is
\[
\Delta_t=
\begin{cases}
I_t-p_q+\epsilon_q\xi_t,&j=q,\\
\xi_t,&j\neq q,
\end{cases}
\qquad \epsilon_q=q^{-3}.
\]
Thus \(\mathbb E_{P_j^{(q)}}[\Delta_t]=0\) in every row, so the causal target fixed by the definition of \(\tau\) is \(\tau=0\).  In post-treatment periods the observed treated outcome is \(Y_t(0)+\Delta_t\), exactly as required by the sampling setup.

Strict stationarity holds in every row because each row is independent and identically distributed over the two-sided time index.  Moreover, for every fixed \(\delta_0>0\), Gaussian moment finiteness, \(0\leq I_t\leq1\), and \(0<\epsilon_q\leq1\) give
\[
\sup_{q\geq1}\sup_{j\geq1}
\mathbb E_{P_j^{(q)}}\lVert X_t\rVert^{8+\delta_0}<\infty.
\]
Choosing \(C_{\mathrm{mom}}\) at least this finite number verifies the declared moment-bound assumption.

We next verify bridge rank and bridge centering rather than assuming them.  For \(e=(1,-1)^{\prime}\), one has the pointwise identities
\[
A_t^{\prime}e=B_t^{\prime}e=U_t=Y_t(0).
\]
For both roles the bridge moment matrix is the symmetric matrix
\[
M_1=\mathbb E[B_tA_t^{\prime}]
=M_2=\mathbb E[A_tB_t^{\prime}]
=
\begin{pmatrix}
3/2&1/2\\
1/2&1/2
\end{pmatrix}.
\]
Its eigenvalues are \(1\pm2^{-1/2}\), so
\[
\sigma_{\min}(M_s)=1-2^{-1/2}>\frac14=\kappa.
\]
Also \(M_se=\mathbb E[Z_{s,t}Y_t(0)]\).  Invertibility and the definition of \(\alpha_s\) therefore imply \(\alpha_s=e\), and hence
\[
Y_t(0)-W_{D_s,t}^{\prime}\alpha_s=0
\quad\text{almost surely},
\qquad s\in\mathcal S.
\]
This proves the bridge-centering condition.  Since \(\mu_s=0\), the definition \(H_s=-\mu_s^{\prime}M_s^{-1}\) also gives \(H_s=0\), whence \(u_{s,t}=0\), \(\psi_{s,t}=0\), and \(A_s=0\) for both roles.

The two ridge populations have the same donor covariance and cross moment,
\[
\Sigma=\mathbb E[A_tA_t^{\prime}]=\mathbb E[B_tB_t^{\prime}]
=\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\1&1\end{pmatrix},
\qquad
b=\mathbb E[A_tU_t]=\mathbb E[B_tU_t]
=\begin{pmatrix}1\\0\end{pmatrix}.
\]
Thus, by the definitions of \(K_s\) and \(a_s\),
\[
K_s=I_2+\Sigma=\begin{pmatrix}3&1\\1&2\end{pmatrix},
\qquad
a_s=K_s^{-1}b=\begin{pmatrix}2/5\\-1/5\end{pmatrix}.
\]
It follows directly from the definition of \(\ell_{s,t}\) that
\[
\ell_{1,t}=\frac{(3U_t-E_t)^2}{25}+\frac15,
\qquad
\ell_{2,t}=\frac{(3U_t-F_t)^2}{25}+\frac15,
\]
and therefore \(L_1=L_2=3/5\) in every row.  Hence
\[
\sup_{j\geq1}\left|\sqrt j(L_{1,j}-L_{2,j})\right|=0,
\]
which verifies the bounded-selector-gap assumption with \(D_{\mathrm{gap}}=0\), and also with any larger fixed envelope.

The centered one-period loss contrast is
\[
\ell_{1,t}-\ell_{2,t}
=\frac{(F_t-E_t)(6U_t-E_t-F_t)}{25}.
\]
The two factors on the right are jointly Gaussian and centered.  Their covariance is zero, while their variances are respectively \(1\) and \(39\); hence they are independent and
\[
\operatorname{Var}(\ell_{1,t}-\ell_{2,t})=\frac{39}{625}.
\]
For completeness, Gaussianity of every required normalized sum follows directly by a characteristic-function expansion.  If \(Z_t\) denotes the centered six-coordinate score vector in any regular row \(j>q\) and \(\Sigma_Z=\operatorname{Var}(Z_t)\), then \(\mathbb E\lVert Z_t\rVert^3<\infty\), and for each fixed vector \(c\),
\[
\mathbb E\exp\!\left\{\frac{\mathrm i c^{\prime}Z_t}{\sqrt j}\right\}
=1-\frac{c^{\prime}\Sigma_Zc}{2j}+O(j^{-3/2}).
\]
Independence over \(t\) gives
\[
\left(1-\frac{c^{\prime}\Sigma_Zc}{2j}+O(j^{-3/2})\right)^j
\longrightarrow \exp\!\left(-\frac12c^{\prime}\Sigma_Zc\right).
\]
Thus the covariance-limit assumption holds and the Gaussian selector coordinate satisfies \(\operatorname{Var}(D)=39/625>\nu\).

For all rows \(j>q\), the exact bridge residual implies \(v_{1,t}=v_{2,t}=\Delta_t=\xi_t\).  Consequently
\[
V_s=\operatorname{Var}(A_s)+r\operatorname{Var}(R_s)=0+1=1>\nu.
\]
The variance-inheritance lemma gives \(V_s^{\mathrm{gap}}=1\), because \(\operatorname{Var}(A_s)=0\).  The limiting stacked covariance is nevertheless singular: both pre-ATT coordinates vanish and the two post-ATT coordinates coincide.  Since, for a fixed \(q\), every row after row \(q\) has this same regular law, the single exceptional row cannot alter any covariance limit.  We have now verified every member condition in the definition of \(\mathcal M(0)\), so \((P_j^{(q)})_{j\geq1}\in\mathcal M(0)\).

It remains to calculate the failure at the exceptional row.  On the late fitting block, the sample bridge equation for role \(1\) has right-hand side
\[
|\mathcal B_q|^{-1}\sum_{t\in\mathcal B_q}B_tY_t(0)
=\left\{|\mathcal B_q|^{-1}\sum_{t\in\mathcal B_q}B_tA_t^{\prime}\right\}e,
\]
and the analogous identity holds for role \(2\).  The displayed random square matrices are invertible almost surely once \(|\mathcal B_q|\geq2\): their determinants are nonzero polynomials of a continuously distributed Gaussian sample and are not identically zero.  Thus the late bridge estimate equals \(e\) exactly for either selected role.  By the construction of the gap-split estimator,
\[
\widehat\tau_{\mathrm{gap}}
=\frac1q\sum_{t=q+1}^{2q}\Delta_t.
\]
The fitted pre-score is identically zero, and the two roles have the same fitted post residual.  The Bartlett standard error is therefore the same for both roles.  It is strictly positive almost surely because \(\epsilon_q>0\), the centered Gaussian perturbation is nonzero almost surely, and the finite Bartlett kernel matrix is positive definite.  Hence the sign of \(T_q\) is the sign of the post-period sample mean, regardless of which \(\mathcal F_A\)-measurable role is selected.

Independence over time makes the post block independent of \(\mathcal F_A\).  Therefore, almost surely,
\[
\Pr_{P_q^{(q)}}\{T_q\leq0\mid\mathcal F_A\}
=\Pr\!\left\{\frac1q\sum_{t=q+1}^{2q}\Delta_t\leq0\right\}.
\]
On the event that every post-period Bernoulli variable is zero, the post mean equals \(-p_q+\epsilon_q\overline\xi_q\), where \(\sqrt q\,\overline\xi_q\sim N(0,1)\).  Consequently
\[
\begin{aligned}
\Pr_{P_q^{(q)}}\{T_q\leq0\mid\mathcal F_A\}
&\geq (1-p_q)^q
\Pr\{\epsilon_q\overline\xi_q\leq p_q\}\\
&=(1-q^{-2})^q\Phi\!\left(\frac{p_q\sqrt q}{\epsilon_q}\right)\\
&=(1-q^{-2})^q\Phi(q^{3/2})\longrightarrow1.
\end{aligned}
\]
Since \(\Phi(0)=1/2\), evaluation of the Kolmogorov supremum at \(x=0\) yields
\[
\begin{aligned}
&\mathbb E_{P_q^{(q)}}\!\left[
\sup_{x\in\mathbb R}
\left|\Pr_{P_q^{(q)}}\{T_q\leq x\mid\mathcal F_A\}-\Phi(x)\right|
\right]\\
&\qquad\geq
\left|\Pr_{P_q^{(q)}}\{T_q\leq0\mid\mathcal F_A\}-\frac12\right|
\longrightarrow\frac12.
\end{aligned}
\]
For each \(q\), the array just constructed is one of the arrays over which the row-\(q\) supremum is taken.  The supremum is therefore bounded below by this diagonal sequence, proving the stated lower bound and the negative answer.  The obstruction is not singular Gaussian mapping: it is that pointwise covariance convergence and limiting variance margins impose no uniform restriction on the row at which the supremum is evaluated.
theorem.justification: The diagonal counterexample identifies the exact quantifier failure in the proposed uniform guarantee.
theorem.gap: Pointwise covariance limits and limiting variance margins do not control the evaluation row uniformly over whole triangular arrays.
theorem.consumer: Any valid split-sample redesign must strengthen the class with uniform rowwise stabilization before claiming uniform selector-conditional inference.
